UNITED STATES OF AMERICA
                                          BEFORE THE
                            FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION


                                                           )
     Southwest Power Pool, Inc.                            )                  Docket No. ER26-247-000
                                                           )


         COMMENTS OF THE SOLAR ENERGY INDUSTRIES ASSOCIATION IN SUPPORT
              The Solar Energy Industries Association (“SEIA”)1 respectfully submits these comments

     in support of Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) proposed revisions to its Open Access

     Transmission Tariff (“SPP Tariff”) to establish a High Impact Large Load (“HILL”) process

     (Attachment BA) and a High Impact Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”) process

     (Attachment BB). Some of SEIA’s members are developing solar and storage resources at scale

     throughout the SPP region to meet rising demand and support the reliable integration of new,

     concentrated large loads. SPP’s proposal creates an innovative, transparent, and reliable pathway

     to interconnect and operate such loads, and to expedite limited, local interconnections of

     supporting generation, while preserving open access principles and protecting other customers.

     The Commission should accept SPP’s filing as just, reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or

     preferential under Section 205 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”), effective January 15, 2026, as

     requested by SPP.


I.            Summary of SPP’s Proposal

              SPP proposes new Attachment BA to define and govern HILLs—large, concentrated

     loads at a single site—and new Attachment BB to establish a separate, expedited, serial study

 process for generation specifically identified for, and limited to, serving a HILL. The HILL

framework layers additional study and ongoing operational requirements on top of existing SPP

Tariff Attachment AQ, Attachment AX, and Attachment Z1 processes to manage the unique

reliability impacts of large loads.2 The HILLGA framework provides a time-limited (5-year

term), localized interconnection service—Load Limited Resource Interconnection Service

(“LLRIS”)—for generation that supports an identified HILL, with increased commercial

readiness and financial commitments to prioritize viable projects and avoid spillover effects to

the Definitive Interconnection System Impact Study (“DISIS”) cluster study process.3

         Attachment BA requires SPP and the Host Transmission Owner to conduct a HILL

Delivery Point Study (“HDPS”) in parallel with AQ/AX studies, expanding beyond traditional

steady-state analysis to include system strength screening, transient stability, and supplemental

Electromagnetic Transient (“EMT”) studies where indicated.4 To ensure cost recovery and deter

speculation, Attachment BA imposes a non-refundable application fee and deposits keyed to

study scope, including a deposit of $100,000 to perform the HDPS and an additional $200,000 if

EMT analysis is necessary, subject to true-up.5 Attachment BA also mandates ongoing

operational and market requirements tailored to large electric loads. Among other measures, SPP

requires installation of phasor measurement recording and communications equipment at the

Transmission Owner’s side of HILL interconnection with phasor measurements to be provided to

the Transmission Provider more frequently than usual SCADA intervals.6 HILLs must register in

the Integrated Marketplace, follow all Non-Conforming Load requirements, provide real-time

 telemetry, maintain remote disconnect capability, and observe an effective ramp rate not

exceeding 20 MW per minute, absent direction.7

         Attachment BB establishes the HILLGA process, delineating the limited service and local

scope of supporting generation. The Tariff specifies that “the HILLGA will evaluate Load

Limited Resource Interconnection Service (LLRIS)… [with] impacts limited to the supported

HILL,” and constrains the point of interconnection to local facilities, including that “the Point of

Interconnection is on the Transmission System no more than two substations away from the

HILL(s) local delivery facilities,” with a one-bus limit at 765 kV transmission facilities.8

HILLGAs are time-limited and do not confer Energy Resource Interconnection Service

(“ERIS”), Network Resource Interconnection Service (“NRIS”), or transmission service.

Interconnection Customers seeking ongoing rights must follow Attachment V for generator

interconnection and obtain transmission service under existing Tariff mechanisms.9

         SPP explains that in order to prioritize viable, shovel-ready projects, Attachment BB

requires a comprehensive set of commercial readiness and financial commitments, including: an

executed HDPS Agreement; a study deposit of $250,000 for requests up to 500 MW and

$500,000 above 500 MW; a security deposit equal to $8,000/MW; a $20,000 application fee

(inflation-adjusted on a triennial schedule); definitive site control milestones (including the POI

substation and tie line); and evidence of at least one specific development milestone at study

agreement execution.10

         SPP also integrates HILL/HILLGA across planning and market frameworks. Attachment

       transmission facilities and clarifies that the list of interconnection facilities and other

      transmission upgrades related to requests for Generator Interconnection Service are approved in

      accordance with the provisions of Attachment V and Attachment BB.11 Attachment AE adds

      registration and data provisions for HILLs and Resources supporting HILLs, including the

      requirement that, under a HILLGIA for LLRIS, “the total Maximum Economic Capacity

      Operating Limits of all supporting Resources [must] not exceed the submitted hourly load

      forecast value of the corresponding HILL,” except under reliability direction or as specified in

      the HILLGIA.12 Conforming revisions to Attachments AQ and AX add HILL-specific data

      elements, dynamic models, and timelines to ensure a consistent process and visibility for study

      and operations.


II.            SPP’s Filing Is Just and Reasonable and Not Unduly Discriminatory or Preferential

               SPP’s proposal satisfies FPA Section 205’s burden of proof and meets the independent

      entity variation standard.13 The HILL/HILLGA framework is narrowly tailored to the unique

      reliability risks of large, concentrated electric loads and integrates targeted study, operational

      visibility, market registration, and localized interconnection service to support those loads

      without compromising open access or the integrity of existing Tariff processes as explained

      below.

               First, the HILL study and operational provisions address genuine reliability needs with

      proportional, transparent requirements. The HDPS deposits and application fee reflect the

 complexity and cost of advanced analyses and are subject to true-up. The EMT screening and

studies, transient stability, and system strength assessments are reasonable given the fast-acting,

power-electronic characteristics of large loads and their concentrated impacts. The PMU

requirement assigns costs to the benefitting entity—the generation resource—and provides high-

fidelity, time-synchronized data necessary to monitor and manage rapid, localized system

dynamics that SCADA alone may not capture utilizing SCADA’s standard four-second update

intervals. The Integrated Marketplace registration, non-conforming load forecasting (including

mandatory intermediate updates), telemetry and remote disconnect capability, and ramp-rate

limits collectively ensure SPP has actionable visibility and control to maintain reliability in real

time.

        Second, HILLGA’s LLRIS is a limited, local interconnection service that neither

displaces nor prejudices the DISIS cluster process. The HILLGA study scope is confined to

serving the identified HILL in the local area. The local interconnection constraints, time-limited

rights, and explicit requirement to pursue ERIS/NRIS under Attachment V for ongoing

interconnection rights (i.e., beyond the five-year term) honor open access principles and ensure

comparability. HILLGA requests are processed on a separate, serial basis and are incorporated

into planning base cases through normal processes; they do not appear in cluster models until

those base cases are updated, thereby avoiding adverse impacts on the timing, priority, and

upgrade allocation of DISIS clusters.

        Third, SPP’s holistic integration across the Tariff ensures transparency, certainty, and

comparability. Attachment O recognizes HILLGA as a source of Network Upgrades, and the

SPP Transmission Expansion Plan will include upgrades from Attachment BB alongside those

from Attachment V. Attachment AE’s HILL-specific registration and operating constraints



                                                  5
 ensure Resources supporting HILLs are operated in alignment with their limited rights and

forecasted load requirements. Attachments AQ and AX incorporate HILL data elements,

dynamic models, and study timelines, ensuring a complete record and consistent treatment across

delivery point assessments and provisional load studies. Attachment J ensures cost allocation and

candidate Incremental Long-Term Congestion Rights eligibility for HILLGA-assigned Network

Upgrades aligned with existing frameworks, avoiding undue discrimination in cost recovery.

       Finally, the proposed timeline and process milestones promote reliable, efficient,

transparent, and timely interconnection consistent with Commission objectives. The HILLGA

System Impact Study is completed no later than 90 calendar days after the review period,

followed by a defined 45-day negotiation window for the HILLGIA and a 10-business-day

tendering period for final agreements. This delineated timeline accelerates capacity additions

needed to serve identified HILLs without compromising good utility practice or the rights of

other customers.

       A final note of caution: SEIA urges SPP to actively monitor and periodically report to the

Commission and to stakeholders on the effectiveness of the HILL and HILLGA frameworks to

meet rising demand and support the reliable integration of new, concentrated large loads and

local interconnection of associated generation resources. SEIA notes that SPP offered the

following commitment:


          SPP’s standard interconnection process (i.e., DISIS) will function unabated to
          achieve the goals outlined in Order Nos. 2003, 2023, and 2023-A.
          …the HILLGA study process will not affect the timing of completing any
          pending DISIS requests because the HILLGA process will be predominantly
          completed by outside consultants paid for by the HILLGA Customer through
          the required study deposits. In this way, the HILLGA process balances the
          need to support HILLS in an expedited manner with the interest of other SPP



                                                6
                Interconnection Customers in a way that is just, reasonable, and consistent with
               open access principles.14
It is essential that SPP honors its pledge to dedicate sufficient resources to continue to meet its

obligations regarding the standard interconnection process and pending DISIS requests. The

Commission should encourage SPP to undertake ongoing monitoring and reporting commitments

regarding its proposed HILLS/HILLGA processes. In addition, SPP did not propose or evaluate

the appropriateness of a sunset provision. SEIA requests that the Commission be vigilant in

exercising its broad investigative and remedial authority under Section 206 of the FPA to ensure

customers with pending or future DISIS requests do not suffer spillover impact or are otherwise

affected by SPP’s implementation of Attachments BA and BB and the coordinated Tariff

revisions.

 III.          Conclusion

              SEIA supports SPP’s proposed additions of Attachments BA and BB and the coordinated

       Tariff revisions. The HILL and HILLGA frameworks are designed to integrate large,

       concentrated loads and enable limited, localized interconnection of supporting generation on an

       expedited basis, while maintaining open access, preserving the integrity of the standard DISIS

       cluster study process, and safeguarding reliability for all customers. The Commission should find

       the proposed Tariff revisions just and reasonable and not unduly discriminatory or preferential,

       and accept them effective January 15, 2026.
